prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Trade, Art, Brain

outputs.L1:
Trade; Trade versus Art.  
Brain; Brain versus Heart.  

Oh, the earthiness of these hard-hearted times,  
When clinking dollars and jingling dimes  
Drown all the finer music of the soul.  

Life stands as an octopus, with but this creed:  
That all the world was made to serve its greed.  
Trade has spread out its mighty, myriad claws  
And drawn into its foul, polluted maw  
The brightest and the best.  

Well-nigh  
Has it drained dry  
The sacred fount of Truth;  
And if, forsooth,  
It has left some struggling streams still free to flow,  
It has so contaminated their course  
That Truth itself is scarcely true.  

Poor Art, with struggling gasp,  
Lies strangled, dying in its mighty grasp;  
It locks its grimy fingers  
About her snowy throat so tender.  

Is there no power to rescue her,  
To protect, defend her?  
Shall Art be left to perish?  
Shall all the images her shrines cherish  
Be left to this iconoclast—  
To vulgar Trade?  

Oh, that mankind had less of Brain and more of Heart.  
Oh, that the world had less of Trade and more of Art.  
Then would there be less grinding down of the poor;  
Then would men learn to love one another more.  

For Trade stalks like a giant through the land,  
Bearing aloft the rich in its high hand,  
While, down beneath its mighty, ponderous tread,  
It crushes those who cry for daily bread.
outputs.L2:
Commerce against Art; intellect against feeling.  
How coarse and pitiless these times have become,  
when the rattle of coins and the chime of money  
overpower the subtler harmonies within the spirit.

Life appears like an octopus, ruled by a single belief:  
that the entire world exists to satisfy its greed.  
Trade has stretched out countless powerful arms  
and pulled into its filthy, tainted mouth  
nearly all that is brightest and noblest.  
It has almost emptied  
the holy spring of Truth;  
and if, indeed,  
a few weak streams still escape from that source,  
their currents have been so poisoned  
that Truth itself is scarcely true anymore.

Poor Art, gasping and fighting for breath,  
is being choked, dying in Trade’s enormous grip.  
Its dirty fingers tighten  
around her delicate white throat.  
Is there no force that can save her, shield her, and defend her?  
Must Art be abandoned to destruction?  
Must all the sacred images treasured in her temples  
be surrendered to this destroyer of idols—this crude Trade?

If only humanity had less cold intellect and more compassion.  
If only the world had less commerce and more Art.  
Then the poor would be oppressed less cruelly;  
people would learn to care for one another more deeply.  
For Trade strides across the country like a giant,  
lifting the wealthy high in his hand,  
while beneath his heavy, crushing footsteps  
he tramples those who plead merely for their daily bread.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a strong condemnation of a materialistic age, one in which the pursuit of money has overwhelmed the deeper and more delicate qualities of human life. Instead of listening to the “music” of the soul—beauty, sympathy, imagination, and moral truth—society has allowed the noise of profit and trade to dominate. The poem suggests that when wealth becomes the highest value, people lose touch with the spiritual and emotional richness that gives life meaning.

Trade is portrayed not as a harmless exchange of goods, but as a greedy and monstrous force. It is shown as something that corrupts truth, distorts human values, and consumes the best parts of humanity. Commerce, in this vision, does not merely organize society; it devours it. The desire for gain becomes so powerful that honesty, compassion, and integrity are sacrificed. The poem therefore presents trade as a force that can turn human beings away from what is noble and toward what is selfish and destructive.

Against this harsh world of money and profit, art appears fragile and endangered. Art represents beauty, imagination, and the higher life of the spirit, but it is threatened by the vulgar power of commerce. The poem suggests that art cannot easily survive in a society that values only what can be bought and sold. It is as if beauty itself is being strangled by materialism, unable to breathe in an atmosphere dominated by greed and calculation.

The speaker’s wish is for humanity to possess more heart and more art, and less cold intellect and trade. This does not mean that reason or commerce have no place in life, but rather that they have become too dominant. The poem argues for a better balance, one in which feeling, creativity, kindness, and moral imagination are valued more highly than profit and cleverness. The speaker longs for a world where human beings are guided not only by the mind and the marketplace, but also by compassion and beauty.

Finally, the poem criticizes the social injustice produced by unchecked commerce. It argues that a society ruled by trade tends to elevate the rich while crushing the poor. Wealth accumulates in the hands of those who already possess power, while the vulnerable are exploited and neglected. In this way, the poem connects materialism not only with spiritual emptiness, but also with inequality and suffering. Its message is that when commerce is allowed to rule without moral restraint, both the human soul and the social order are damaged.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a powerful condemnation of a society ruled by commerce and material gain. It imagines Trade not as a neutral part of everyday life, but as a living, destructive force: greedy, aggressive, and morally corrupt. Through vivid personification, Trade becomes almost monstrous, a power that distorts truth, exploits the poor, and reduces human life to profit and calculation. In this world, honesty is weakened, compassion is ignored, and those who are already vulnerable are crushed beneath the demands of wealth and competition.

The poem also suggests that commerce does not merely harm people economically; it damages the human spirit. Art, beauty, imagination, and emotional depth are all threatened by a culture that values money above everything else. Art is portrayed as being strangled or silenced by the harsh rule of profit, while the finer qualities of life are pushed aside. The poem therefore criticizes a society that worships intellect, efficiency, and gain while forgetting tenderness, creativity, and moral responsibility.

Against this bleak vision, the poem offers an alternative. It argues that human beings must replace cold self-interest with compassion, sympathy, and artistic feeling. If people allowed love, beauty, and imagination to guide their actions, society would become more humane and more just. Art would no longer be suppressed, truth would be protected, and the poor would no longer be sacrificed to the ambitions of the wealthy. The poem ultimately calls for a world in which beauty is preserved, human love is deepened, and social life is shaped not by greed, but by kindness and spiritual richness.
outputs.L5:
Trade, art, and the brain are deeply connected in the way humans create value, share ideas, and understand the world. Trade is not only the exchange of goods and services; it is also an exchange of culture, imagination, and knowledge. Throughout history, trade routes carried more than spices, fabrics, and tools—they carried artistic styles, symbols, stories, and new ways of thinking.

Art plays a powerful role in this process because it communicates across borders and languages. A painting, sculpture, song, or design can express emotions and ideas that words sometimes cannot. When art moves through trade, it influences other cultures and inspires new forms of creativity. For example, patterns from one region may appear in the textiles of another, or musical instruments may evolve as they travel between communities.

The brain is at the center of both trade and art. It helps people recognize beauty, solve problems, make decisions, and imagine new possibilities. In trade, the brain evaluates risk, trust, and value. In art, it responds to color, rhythm, shape, and meaning. Creativity and decision-making both depend on the brain’s ability to connect ideas in original ways.

Together, trade, art, and the brain show how human progress is built on exchange and imagination. Trade spreads materials and ideas, art transforms them into meaningful expression, and the brain makes it all possible through creativity, memory, and understanding. This connection reminds us that commerce is not only economic—it is also cultural and deeply human.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style protest poem contrasting commerce with art, using personification of Trade as a monstrous force crushing truth, beauty, and the poor.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Mammon Engine**

O England, robed in coal-smoke’s funeral pall,  
Whose chimneys write their midnight on the skies,  
Hark! through thy marts I hear a brazen call,  
Where Trade, red-eyed, in iron harness lies.  

He strides abroad—a giant foul and vast,  
With ledgers for his heart, and wheels for breath;  
His shadow makes the meadow’s green aghast,  
His footstep is the arithmetic of death.  

He grinds the dawn to cinders in his mill,  
He coins the sunset into sordid gold;  
The singing stream, obedient to his will,  
Creeps black beneath his factories, bought and sold.  

Truth, pale and crowned with stars, he drags through mire;  
He laughs to see her sacred garments torn.  
Beauty, whose touch once set the soul on fire,  
He starves beside the road, and names her scorn.  

And Art—poor Art! with heaven in her eyes,  
Who bears the lyre and lamp from age to age—  
He bids her paint his wares, applaud his lies,  
And gild the bars of Labour’s living cage.  

Beneath his wheels the children’s faces fade,  
Their little hands grow old with toil and pain;  
The widow’s prayer, the workman’s humble trade,  
Are trampled flat beneath his golden train.  

“Profit!” he roars; the bells of mercy cease.  
“Market!” he cries; the poet’s voice is drowned.  
He sells the very olive-branch of peace,  
And weighs the human heartbeat by the pound.  

Yet still, above the counting-house’s din,  
A purer music trembles, faint but clear:  
The soul of Man, unpurchased from within,  
The deathless note that tyrants hate to hear.  

Rise, then, O Art! take back thy ravished throne;  
Let Truth unveil her forehead to the sun;  
Let Beauty claim the world as still her own,  
And speak for those whose bread is hardly won.  

For gold shall rust, and iron empires fall,  
And Trade’s huge idol crumble into sand;  
But song shall answer still the ages’ call,  
And lift the poor with one immortal hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic free-verse poem titled “Trade versus Art, Brain versus Heart” about capitalism strangling creativity and compassion.
counterfactuals.output:
# Trade versus Art, Brain versus Heart

In the market square,  
the violinist tightens one string  
until it snaps.

Above him, glass towers  
count the echoes.

Every note is weighed,  
every color appraised,  
every trembling hand  
asked to submit a forecast.

The painters are told  
to make their grief scalable.  
The poets are advised  
to optimize sorrow.  
The dancers must prove  
their hunger converts.

Somewhere, a child draws a sun  
with too many rays,  
and a committee gathers  
to discuss efficiency.

There is a ledger  
where a heart should be.

There is a clock  
pressed against the throat  
of every unfinished song.

Capital, with its polished shoes,  
walks through the garden  
naming each flower  
an asset,  
each bee  
a unit of labor,  
each orchard  
a quarterly promise.

And compassion—  
that old, barefoot saint—  
stands outside the boardroom  
with rain in her hair,  
holding out bread  
no one has monetized.

The brain, sharpened into a blade,  
calculates the cost of mercy.  
The heart, bruised but burning,  
answers in a language  
without invoices.

What is the price  
of a mother’s sleepless prayer?  
What is the margin  
on a stranger’s hand  
reaching through smoke?

The machine does not understand  
why the mural refuses  
to become a billboard,  
why the song keeps turning  
toward the wounded,  
why the human voice  
still breaks beautifully  
when it tells the truth.

So it tightens.  
It buys the stage,  
brands the silence,  
leases the dream back  
to the dreamer.

But under the pavement,  
roots conspire.

In back rooms, basements,  
subway tunnels, kitchens,  
the unprofitable still gather—  
passing poems like contraband,  
painting doors on prison walls,  
feeding one another  
with songs too wild  
to be owned.

Trade raises its fist.  
Art opens its ribs.

The brain builds a cage  
of reason and return.  
The heart slips through  
as fire,  
as water,  
as a red bird  
no currency can catch.

And when the towers fall quiet,  
when the ledgers rot,  
when the last advertisement  
for salvation  
flickers out—

someone will be singing.

Not for profit.  
Not for permission.  
But because the world,  
half-strangled,  
still has breath,

and breath,  
given freely,  
becomes music.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an old-fashioned moral poem in the style of late 19th-century social criticism, lamenting how money and greed have polluted truth and destroyed art.
counterfactuals.output:
**Mammon’s Lantern**

In former days, when hearths were low  
And lamps burned dim but clear,  
Men prized the word that, whispered slow,  
Could make the conscience hear.  
The poet walked with threadbare coat,  
Yet bore a kingly part;  
For truth was silver in his throat,  
And God was in his art.

But now the mart’s unholy bell  
Rings louder than the chime;  
And men who have their souls to sell  
Are counted men of time.  
The ledger lies where Scripture lay,  
The coin usurps the creed;  
And honor, dressed in worn array,  
Goes begging where they feed.

The painter dips his brush in gold,  
Not sunrise, blood, or tears;  
He frames the flattery of the bold,  
And gilds their little years.  
The singer tunes his sacred strings  
To please a purchaser’s nod,  
And trims the strong, immortal wings  
That once aspired to God.

Truth stands outside the banquet gate,  
With dust upon her hair;  
While Falsehood, robed in rich estate,  
Sits laughing in the chair.  
The critic weighs with merchant scales  
The dreams no scale should test;  
And beauty, when the auction fails,  
Is thrust among the rest.

O age of iron crowned with brass,  
O city loud and blind,  
How swiftly do thy triumphs pass,  
How poor the wealth they find!  
For gold may build the marble hall  
And buy the flattering tongue,  
But cannot hear the inward call  
That made the ancients young.

Return, return, ye sons of men,  
Before the lamps expire;  
Take up the honest word again,  
And guard the altar-fire.  
Let art be poor, but not profaned;  
Let truth be stern, yet free;  
For all that Mammon’s hand has gained  
Is dust beneath the sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a passionate poetic monologue where “Trade” is an octopus-like villain and “Art” is an innocent figure being strangled, ending with a plea for more heart and less brain.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold Trade, that many-armed tyrant of the deep—  
slick with ink, jeweled with coin,  
his thousand suckers kissing every surface  
only to leave it poorer.

He rises from the market’s black water  
with ledgers for eyes,  
with contracts coiled like tentacles,  
with a smile measured in percentages.  
He does not sing—he calculates.  
He does not dream—he inventories.  
He wraps himself around the world  
and calls the squeezing “growth.”

And there—  
there is Art.

Barefoot, bright-eyed,  
holding a trembling candle in both hands,  
a child of breath and color,  
of bruised violins and unfinished poems,  
of murals on cracked walls,  
of songs hummed by the lonely  
so they might not vanish entirely.

Art does not bargain well.  
Art forgets the price of itself.  
Art gives away its bread,  
spills its gold into the mouths of strangers,  
kneels in the dust to draw wings  
on the shadows of the defeated.

So Trade descends.

One arm around the throat:  
“Will it sell?”  
Another around the ribs:  
“Who is the audience?”  
Another over the mouth:  
“Make it simpler.”  
Another over the eyes:  
“Make it safer.”  
Another at the wrist:  
“Make it faster.”  
Another at the heart:  
“Make it useful.”

And Art—poor radiant Art—  
gasps beneath the pressure,  
its colors dimming,  
its music thinning into jingles,  
its wild forests trimmed into logos,  
its sacred fire bottled, branded,  
stacked neatly on a shelf.

O monstrous Trade!  
Must every rose become a receipt?  
Must every cry be polished into product?  
Must wonder beg permission  
from the cold arithmetic of gain?

Look how Art still reaches—  
even now, strangled,  
even now, shaking—  
toward the human face,  
toward the wound,  
toward the impossible dawn.

Do not let the octopus win.  
Do not let the candle drown.  
Loosen the grip.  
Break the ledger’s spell.  
Let beauty breathe again.

Give us less counting and more trembling,  
less machinery and more mercy,  
less hunger for profit and more hunger for truth—  
please,  
more heart  
and less brain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long, ornate poem condemning materialism, clinking dollars, and the oppression of the poor, while praising art, truth, and human love.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Hymn Against the Golden Idol**

I.

O age of brazen arithmetic,  
O city crowned with chimneys and with glass,  
Where morning breaks not like a rose  
But like a ledger opened under ash—  
How loudly in thy temples ring  
The little bells of minted greed!  
How bright the dollars clink and sing,  
Like insects in a hollow reed,  
While, underneath their silver chime,  
The human heart is crushed for time.

The counting-house has learned to pray  
With fingers cold upon its beads;  
It blesses interest, crowns delay,  
And fattens upon widows’ needs.  
It makes a scripture out of price,  
A gospel out of gain;  
It sets its altar upon ice  
And calls compassion vain.  
There Mercy stands, in tattered shawl,  
Outside the banquet’s bolted hall,  
While inside, flushed with stolen wine,  
The golden idol’s candles shine.

II.

Listen—the dollars clink, clink, clink,  
Like chains in some subterranean mine;  
They dance along the polished brink  
Of tables set with fruit and wine.  
They clink in pockets soft as sin,  
They clink in vaults where daylight dies,  
They clink above the beggar’s skin,  
They clink beneath the merchant’s lies.  
Small moons of metal, round and cold,  
They eclipse the sun of the soul;  
They turn the warmest hand to gold  
And make the living spirit coal.

For every coin that brightly spins  
Upon the banker’s marble floor,  
Some child grows thin, some mother pins  
A threadbare hope outside the door.  
For every tower that climbs the sky,  
Its windows blazing, proud, immense,  
A thousand nameless sleepers lie  
Against the walls of opulence.  
For every feast where laughter pours  
Like honey from the gilded room,  
A hunger walks on tenement floors  
And counts the cracks in borrowed gloom.

III.

O Wealth, thou wolf in ermine dressed,  
Thou serpent with a jeweled head,  
How many sorrows have caressed  
The pillow where thy limbs are spread?  
How many backs have bent to lift  
Thy palaces from clay and smoke?  
How many dreams were sold as thrift,  
How many spirits bent and broke?  
Thy wheels roll on; beneath their tread  
The poor are dust, the weak are clay;  
Thy heralds cry, “The world is fed!”  
While empty bowls are turned away.

Thou speakest of “markets,” “laws,” and “needs,”  
Of “order,” “progress,” “destiny,”  
Yet behind those velvet words one reads  
The old decree of tyranny.  
The hand that cannot pay is bound,  
The mouth that begs is told to wait;  
The feet that bleed upon the ground  
Are blamed for standing at the gate.  
And Poverty, that patient queen  
In rags more royal than thy rings,  
Is mocked by those whose eyes have seen  
No winter except through windowed wings.

IV.

But cursed be the heart that hears  
The poor man’s cough and turns away;  
Cursed be the feast that disappears  
Before the orphan’s face of clay.  
Cursed be the crown of glittering things  
That buys a child’s unwritten years;  
Cursed be the palace with its wings  
Built from another’s blood and tears.  
Cursed be the doctrine, sleek and cold,  
That measures man by what he owns;  
Cursed be the lips that praise their gold  
Above the music of human moans.

For man is more than appetite,  
More than the hunger to possess;  
He is a lamp in mortal night,  
A question clothed in tenderness.  
He is the dream that lifts the stone,  
The song that outlives empires’ breath;  
He is not meant to kneel alone  
Before the cashbox, crowned with death.  
No soul was born to be a gear  
In engines grinding bread to dust;  
No hand was shaped for endless fear,  
No brow for ashes, debt, and rust.

V.

Bring forth the painters with their flames,  
The poets with their thundered flowers,  
The sculptors whispering secret names  
To marble in its moonlit hours.  
Bring forth the violins that weep  
With all the grief the world conceals;  
Bring forth the songs that sow and reap  
More truth than iron ever feels.  
For Art, that luminous rebel, stands  
With sunrise hidden in her hair;  
She breaks the tyrant’s measuring hands  
And fills the beggar’s cup with air—

Not empty air, but breath made bright,  
The common wind of hope and speech;  
She opens windows into light  
No price can buy, no vault can reach.  
She takes the laborer’s broken day  
And frames it in a golden dawn;  
She hears what systems cast away  
And makes a music of the pawn.  
She kneels beside the voiceless poor  
And gives their silence trumpet-tone;  
She writes upon the factory door:  
“No human sorrow walks alone.”

VI.

O Truth, austere and shining bride,  
Thou dost not wear the merchant’s chain;  
No auctioneer may set thy pride  
Upon a block for private gain.  
Thou art the star above the mast  
When all the seas of falsehood roll;  
Thou art the bread that cannot last  
Unless divided soul to soul.  
Thou dost not flatter thrones nor banks,  
Nor gild the lies of comfortable men;  
Thou walkest through the pauper ranks  
And makest prophets there again.

Truth stands where hungry children stand,  
Where women stitch till candles drown,  
Where men with scarred and faithful hands  
Build roofs beneath which they lie down  
Unsheltered in the rain of debt,  
Unwarmed by all the fires they made.  
Truth does not permit us to forget  
The worker in the wealth parade.  
Truth tears the satin veil apart,  
And in the mirror of the street  
Shows us our own divided heart—  
Half banquet, and half bleeding feet.

VII.

And Love—O Love, thou final law,  
Thou rose that roots in common earth,  
Thou tender lightning without flaw,  
Thou measure of a human worth—  
Rise now against the iron creed  
That makes a god of getting more;  
Rise like spring through winter’s greed,  
Rise like the sea against the shore.  
Let no one eat while others starve;  
Let no one sleep while others freeze;  
Let no one’s comfort boldly carve  
Its luxuries from another’s knees.

Love is not sentimental smoke,  
Not perfumed sigh, not idle grace;  
It is the shoulder at the yoke,  
The lamp held to a stranger’s face.  
It is the bread in two hands broken,  
The coat removed in bitter snow,  
The dangerous and honest token  
That none are free while some lie low.  
It is the mother’s midnight tread,  
The comrade’s arm, the healer’s art;  
The vow that all shall yet be fed  
By courage of the human heart.

VIII.

Then let the clinking dollars cease  
Their insect music in the hall;  
Let justice, not the lust of increase,  
Be carved above the market wall.  
Let wages bloom like fields of grain;  
Let labor’s children laugh and learn;  
Let no one drink another’s pain,  
Let no one’s grief be called return.  
Let factories open to the sun,  
Let mines be emptied of despair;  
Let bread be earned by everyone  
And dignity breathe everywhere.

Let mansions loosen all their locks,  
Let gardens overrun the street;  
Let bankers hear in vaults and stocks  
The marching of unpurchased feet.  
Let paper crowns and golden bars  
Grow pale before a worker’s face;  
Let human need, not hungry stars  
Of profit, shape the common place.  
For wealth that does not serve the whole  
Is rot beneath a jeweled rind;  
And luxury that starves a soul  
Is poverty of humankind.

IX.

O artists, lift your lanterns high!  
O lovers, join your hands and sing!  
O tellers of the unsold truth, defy  
The coin that calls itself a king.  
Paint not for parlors blind with ease  
Alone, but for the shivering lane;  
Write not to please the gilded knees  
That kneel to vanity and gain.  
Sing so the sleeping rich may start,  
And hear beyond their velvet wall  
The accusation of the heart,  
The human summons, vast and tall.

Make beauty not a private throne  
Where weary multitudes may not tread;  
Make beauty bread, and more than bread—  
A fire where frozen souls are fed.  
Let every canvas, chord, and line  
Refuse the tyrannies of price;  
Let every true and tender sign  
Defy the market’s sacrifice.  
For art is not a trinket sold  
To decorate a banquet’s shame;  
It is the poor man’s hidden gold,  
The exile’s country, freedom’s flame.

X.

I dream a dawn beyond the smoke  
Where no child’s tears are counted cheap,  
Where no one lives beneath the yoke  
That others wear only in sleep;  
Where coins are tools and not commands,  
Where trade is servant, never lord;  
Where honest work and open hands  
Are dearer than the miser’s hoard.  
I dream a city built on care,  
With schools like orchards, homes like songs,  
Where justice moves through common air  
And heals the old arithmetic wrongs.

There, truth shall walk in linen plain,  
And art shall blossom in the square;  
There, love shall be the civic grain,  
The daily bread, the public prayer.  
No golden idol, squat and dumb,  
Shall rule the temple of the day;  
No clinking dollars there shall numb  
The music of the human clay.  
For every soul shall be a lyre,  
And every hand a kindled star;  
The world shall warm itself at fire  
No vault can keep, no lock can bar.

XI.

Until that dawn, let voices rise  
Like bells from towers not yet built;  
Let conscience trouble banquet skies  
And thunder over perfumed guilt.  
Let poets fling their scarlet seed  
In furrows where the poor have trod;  
Let truth uproot the weed of greed,  
Let love unmake the money-god.  
Let every street become a page,  
Let every tear become a vow,  
Let every hunger in this age  
Be crowned with bread, beginning now.

O heart, reject the gilded lie  
That life is measured, weighed, and priced.  
The soul was made to sing, to try  
The difficult mercy, unenticed  
By clinking coins and jeweled dust,  
By market thrones and selfish ease.  
The soul was made for bread and trust,  
For open hands, for living trees,  
For art that lifts, for truth that frees,  
For love that kneels and does not cease—  
Until the poorest child may stand  
Unfrightened in the morning land,  
And all the earth, from shore to shore,  
Be rich in justice evermore.
